overview.lesson_purpose: Develop a reliable method for reconstructing the single correct order of jumbled academic text boxes by combining meaning, grammar, reference, and discourse clues.
overview.estimated_study_time: Plan for about 2 hours of focused study for this chapter.
overview.item_type_summary: In Re-order paragraphs, several text boxes from one academic passage appear in the wrong order. The test taker must arrange them so that the passage develops logically and cohesively.
overview.main_skill_focus: The task primarily tests understanding of text organization and cohesion rather than isolated vocabulary knowledge.
text_features_to_analyze: The main topic and the most independent opening sentence
The movement from general ideas to supporting details
References created by articles, pronouns, demonstratives, and repeated nouns
Logical relationships signalled by discourse markers
Chronological, procedural, causal, comparative, and problem-solution structures
The consistency of tense, vocabulary, and topic across sentence boundaries
overview.success_principle: Do not try to guess the complete order immediately. Build the passage by identifying a strong opening sentence, forming reliable sentence pairs, joining those pairs into a chain, and then checking the whole paragraph.

learning_goals: Identify a likely topic sentence that can introduce the passage without depending on earlier information.
Distinguish general statements from examples, explanations, evidence, consequences, and conclusions.
Use indefinite and definite articles to track first mention and later reference.
Resolve pronouns and reference expressions by locating their correct antecedents.
Recognize discourse markers for addition, contrast, similarity, examples, cause and effect, sequence, generalization, and conclusion.
Follow logical, chronological, procedural, and argumentative development across several text boxes.
Form strong adjacent sentence pairs before attempting to finalize the complete sequence.
Reject possible orders that create an unexplained pronoun, missing noun, broken timeline, repeated introduction, or illogical transition.
Complete practice items efficiently under shared Reading-section time pressure.
Explain why each sentence belongs in its selected position rather than relying only on intuition.

core_method.name: OPEN-PAIR-CHAIN-CHECK
core_method.purpose: A repeatable method for solving Re-order paragraphs accurately and quickly.

steps.name: Preview every box
steps.instruction: Read all text boxes once for the general subject. Do not begin dragging boxes after reading only the first one.
steps.example: Notice whether the passage is about a building, a historical event, a scientific process, a social issue, or a research finding.

steps.name: Find the opening candidate
steps.instruction: Choose the sentence that introduces the topic most independently and contains the fewest backward references.
steps.example: A sentence naming the Burj Dubai is a stronger opening than one beginning with 'The building' because the building must first be identified.

steps.name: Mark dependent beginnings
steps.instruction: Identify boxes beginning with pronouns, definite noun phrases, contrast markers, result markers, examples, or conclusions. These usually require earlier information.
steps.example: 'They', 'this method', 'the study', 'however', 'therefore', and 'in conclusion' rarely function as independent openings.

steps.name: Build strong pairs
steps.instruction: Find two sentences with a clear grammatical or semantic connection. Prefer exact links over broad topic similarity.
steps.example: 'A hotel occupies several floors' is likely to precede 'That accommodation offers panoramic views' because 'that accommodation' refers back to the hotel.

steps.name: Join pairs into a chain
steps.instruction: Combine reliable pairs by following the passage's development from introduction to explanation, evidence, consequence, and conclusion.
steps.example: General claim → explanation → example → result is usually more coherent than example → general claim → unrelated result.

steps.name: Check global logic
steps.instruction: Read the proposed order as one paragraph and test whether its topic, tense, references, and argument develop smoothly.
steps.example: A sentence describing the consequences of an experiment should not appear before the experiment itself has been introduced.

steps.name: Use elimination for uncertain gaps
steps.instruction: When two positions remain uncertain, compare which option creates fewer broken references or weaker transitions.
steps.example: Reject an order if 'this early Pope' appears before any Pope has been named.

steps.name: Finalize efficiently
steps.instruction: Once every adjacent link has a defensible reason, submit and move on rather than repeatedly rearranging a coherent answer.
steps.example: A complete chain supported by article, referent, and discourse clues is stronger than a late change based only on how one sentence sounds.

techniques.name: Topic-sentence test
techniques.teaching_point: The opening sentence usually introduces the subject, provides necessary background, and does not rely heavily on earlier text.
how_to_apply: Look for a named person, place, theory, event, problem, or phenomenon.
Prefer a general statement over a detailed example.
Avoid sentences beginning with unexplained pronouns or demonstratives.
Check whether the sentence would make sense to a reader seeing the topic for the first time.
techniques.example: The sentence 'Valentine's Day has developed from several historical traditions' can open a paragraph more naturally than 'The holiday later became associated with romantic love.'

techniques.name: General-to-specific development
techniques.teaching_point: Academic paragraphs commonly move from a broad claim to explanation, evidence, examples, and implications.
how_to_apply: Identify the broadest statement.
Place definitions after the term or concept they explain.
Place statistics or examples after the relevant claim.
Place interpretations or consequences after the evidence.
techniques.example: Renewable energy is expanding rapidly → several governments have introduced incentives → solar installations increased by 30 percent → this growth has reduced dependence on imported fuel.

techniques.name: Article tracking
techniques.teaching_point: Articles can distinguish new information from information already known to the reader.
how_to_apply: Treat 'a' or 'an' as a possible first introduction.
Treat 'the' as a possible later reference to something already introduced.
Check whether a superlative such as 'the largest' depends on an established category.
Do not assume that every sentence with an indefinite article must come first; meaning still controls the order.
techniques.example: 'A hotel is located on the upper floors' normally comes before 'The hotel contains more than 150 rooms.'

techniques.name: Pronoun and antecedent matching
techniques.teaching_point: A pronoun must normally follow a compatible noun or noun phrase.
how_to_apply: Match singular pronouns such as 'it' with a singular antecedent.
Match plural pronouns such as 'they' or 'these' with a plural antecedent.
Check whether human pronouns refer to people and non-human pronouns refer to objects or concepts.
Confirm that the nearest possible antecedent also makes logical sense.
techniques.example: 'Researchers interviewed 300 athletes' should precede 'They were asked about motivation and training habits.'

techniques.name: Demonstrative-reference tracking
techniques.teaching_point: Expressions such as 'this process', 'that result', 'these findings', and 'such behaviour' summarize or rename earlier information.
how_to_apply: Identify the noun inside the reference phrase.
Ask what earlier idea could logically be described by that noun.
Place the reference immediately after or close to its source.
Reject distant or vague antecedents when a clearer connection exists.
techniques.example: 'The experiment produced an unexpected decline in performance' is a likely predecessor of 'This result challenged the original theory.'

techniques.name: Lexical-chain recognition
techniques.teaching_point: Writers maintain cohesion by repeating key words or replacing them with synonyms, categories, and related expressions.
how_to_apply: Circle repeated content words.
Look for a specific noun followed by a broader category.
Look for synonyms or paraphrases that continue the same idea.
Distinguish a genuine lexical chain from sentences that merely share the same broad topic.
techniques.example: Pope Gelasius I → this early Pope → the religious leader forms a stronger chain than three sentences that only contain the word 'history'.

techniques.name: Discourse-marker mapping
techniques.teaching_point: Linking expressions reveal how a sentence relates to previous information.
how_to_apply: Place example markers after a general claim.
Place contrast markers after an idea that can be opposed or qualified.
Place result markers after a cause or supporting evidence.
Place conclusion markers near the end of an argument.
techniques.example: 'The policy reduced short-term costs. However, it created several long-term problems.'

techniques.name: Chronology and tense control
techniques.teaching_point: Historical and procedural texts often contain time expressions and tense patterns that restrict the possible order.
how_to_apply: Arrange explicit dates from earlier to later unless the writer deliberately uses a flashback.
Place 'initially', 'first', and 'at the beginning' before later stages.
Place 'subsequently', 'later', and 'eventually' after earlier developments.
Check whether past-perfect forms describe events that occurred before another past event.
techniques.example: The festival existed in pagan society → Pope Gelasius later replaced it with a Christian celebration → the holiday eventually became associated with romantic love.

techniques.name: Cause-and-effect linking
techniques.teaching_point: A result sentence requires an earlier cause, condition, action, or piece of evidence.
how_to_apply: Identify result markers such as 'therefore', 'thus', and 'as a result'.
Ask what exact event produced the result.
Check whether the cause is sufficient and logically compatible.
Keep the result close to the cause unless another sentence explains the mechanism.
techniques.example: Heavy rainfall continued for several days → the river exceeded its normal level → as a result, nearby roads were closed.

techniques.name: Contrast and concession linking
techniques.teaching_point: Contrast markers connect ideas that differ, qualify each other, or create an unexpected relationship.
how_to_apply: Find the statement being contradicted or limited.
Check whether the contrast is direct rather than merely a change of topic.
Place 'however' after a complete contrasting idea.
Recognize concession patterns such as 'although X, Y' and 'despite X, Y'.
techniques.example: The new system is cheaper to operate. Nevertheless, many institutions have been slow to adopt it.

techniques.name: Paragraph-role labeling
techniques.teaching_point: Assigning a function to each box reduces dependence on intuition.
how_to_apply: Label each sentence as introduction, definition, explanation, example, evidence, contrast, result, or conclusion.
Compare the labels with common academic patterns.
Avoid placing a conclusion before the evidence it summarizes.
Use the labels to distinguish two sentences that appear equally possible.
techniques.example: Introduction → definition → example → evaluation is more plausible than evaluation → example → introduction → definition.

techniques.name: Adjacent-pair prioritization
techniques.teaching_point: A correct order is usually easier to construct from strong local links than from a single guess about the whole paragraph.
how_to_apply: Search for exact noun-pronoun links.
Search for claim-example and cause-result links.
Lock only pairs supported by strong evidence.
Leave weakly connected sentences movable until the main chain is clear.
techniques.example: If B introduces 'a scientific survey' and D begins 'the survey', treat B-D as a strong pair before deciding where that pair belongs globally.

worked_examples.title: Burj Dubai: articles and backward reference

jumbled_sentences.text: A hotel is also located within the building.
The Burj Dubai was designed to become one of the tallest structures in the world.
That accommodation occupies several of its upper floors.
The building's final height was initially estimated from published construction statistics.
The use of the word 'estimated' reflected uncertainty about the completed structure.

guided_reasoning: B is the best opening because it names and introduces the Burj Dubai.
D follows because 'the building' refers back to the Burj Dubai.
E follows D because 'the word estimated' refers to the wording used in D.
A introduces new information with 'a hotel'.
C follows A because 'that accommodation' refers back to the hotel.
worked_examples.transfer_rule: Track first mention, later reference, and renamed reference: proper name → the building → a hotel → that accommodation.

worked_examples.title: Valentine's Day: referents across historical stages

jumbled_sentences.text: This pagan festival was connected with fertility and the arrival of spring.
The holiday later became associated with expressions of romantic love.
Pope Gelasius I eventually replaced the celebration with a Christian observance.
Valentine's Day appears to have developed from an earlier Roman celebration.
This early Pope helped reshape the meaning of the event.

guided_reasoning: D introduces Valentine's Day and the earlier Roman celebration.
A follows because 'this pagan festival' refers to that Roman celebration.
C introduces Pope Gelasius I and describes a later historical action.
E follows because 'this early Pope' refers directly to Pope Gelasius I.
B completes the development by explaining what the holiday later became.
worked_examples.transfer_rule: A demonstrative phrase cannot be resolved until its source has appeared: celebration → this pagan festival; Pope Gelasius I → this early Pope.

worked_examples.title: Research study: claim, method, finding, interpretation

jumbled_sentences.text: These findings suggest that regular movement may support concentration as well as physical health.
Researchers have increasingly examined the relationship between exercise and academic performance.
The students who exercised regularly completed the attention task more accurately.
In one study, university students reported their weekly activity and then completed a computerized attention task.
However, the researchers warned that the study did not prove that exercise directly caused the improvement.

guided_reasoning: B introduces the broad research topic.
D provides a specific example signalled by 'in one study'.
C reports the result of the study described in D.
A interprets the result through 'these findings'.
E qualifies the interpretation with a contrast marker and a methodological warning.
worked_examples.transfer_rule: A common research pattern is topic → study method → result → interpretation → limitation.

worked_examples.title: Urban transport: problem and response

jumbled_sentences.text: As a result, several city governments have expanded public transport and cycling infrastructure.
Rapid urban growth has increased traffic congestion in many major cities.
These alternatives can reduce the number of private vehicles entering crowded centres.
The problem also contributes to air pollution, travel delays, and higher fuel consumption.
Nevertheless, their success depends on affordability, reliability, and public acceptance.

guided_reasoning: B introduces the central urban problem.
D continues it through 'the problem' and adds consequences.
A presents a response through the result marker 'as a result'.
C explains the value of 'these alternatives', referring to public transport and cycling infrastructure.
E adds a final qualification through 'nevertheless' and 'their success'.
worked_examples.transfer_rule: Problem → consequences → response → benefit → limitation is a frequent academic structure.

worked_examples.title: Scientific process: chronological sequence

jumbled_sentences.text: Eventually, the water vapour cools and forms clouds.
The cycle begins when heat from the sun causes surface water to evaporate.
After condensation, water returns to the ground as precipitation.
The resulting vapour rises into the atmosphere.
Some of this water then flows into rivers, lakes, and oceans, allowing the process to begin again.

guided_reasoning: B explicitly marks the beginning of the process.
D follows because 'the resulting vapour' is created by evaporation.
A describes what eventually happens to the vapour.
C follows condensation and describes precipitation.
E completes the cycle and refers back to the water that has returned to the ground.
worked_examples.transfer_rule: For processes, follow the physical transformation and use sequence markers as confirmation.

worked_examples.title: Opening-sentence elimination

jumbled_sentences.text: However, this interpretation has been challenged by more recent evidence.
The theory was first proposed to explain why the population declined.
This evidence came from newly analyzed archaeological remains.
For many years, researchers accepted a single explanation for the decline of the population.

guided_reasoning: A cannot open because 'however' contrasts with an earlier position and 'this interpretation' needs an antecedent.
B is possible grammatically, but 'the theory' sounds like a known theory and is more specific than D.
D independently establishes the topic and the accepted explanation.
B develops the explanation by identifying the purpose of the theory.
A introduces a challenge, and C identifies the evidence mentioned in A.
worked_examples.transfer_rule: Eliminate opening candidates with unresolved contrast, definite reference, or demonstrative reference before comparing the remaining independent sentences.

option_elimination_phrases: This cannot be first because the reference has no antecedent.
This pair is weak because the repeated topic does not create a direct link.
This sentence requires an earlier cause, example, or contrasting idea.
This order introduces 'the' before the noun has been established.
This position breaks the chronological sequence.
This option repeats the introduction instead of developing it.
This transition is grammatically possible but logically unsupported.
The alternative creates a clearer adjacent connection.
reasoning_phrases: Sentence B introduces the noun that sentence D refers to.
The pronoun in this sentence points back to the plural noun in the previous box.
The example marker shows that a general statement must come earlier.
The result marker requires the preceding sentence to provide a cause.
The final sentence summarizes rather than introduces the argument.
The tense and time expression place this event after the earlier stage.

common_mistakes.mistake: Choosing the first sentence only because it sounds broad.
common_mistakes.why_it_fails: A sentence may sound general but still contain a hidden backward reference such as 'the issue', 'this approach', or 'however'.
common_mistakes.correction: Apply both tests: the sentence should be broad enough to introduce the topic and independent enough to require no earlier information.

common_mistakes.mistake: Assuming a sentence with 'the' can safely begin.
common_mistakes.why_it_fails: The definite article often marks information already introduced.
common_mistakes.correction: Search for an earlier sentence that names or introduces the noun with a proper name, 'a', or 'an'.

common_mistakes.mistake: Assuming every sentence with 'a' or 'an' must appear first.
common_mistakes.why_it_fails: An indefinite article may introduce a new supporting example in the middle of a passage.
common_mistakes.correction: Use article clues together with paragraph role and overall meaning.

common_mistakes.mistake: Interpreting pronouns without locating an exact antecedent.
common_mistakes.why_it_fails: A pronoun may match several nouns grammatically but only one logically.
common_mistakes.correction: Check number, meaning, distance, and whether the proposed antecedent produces a natural sentence pair.

common_mistakes.mistake: Ordering sentences because they contain similar vocabulary.
common_mistakes.why_it_fails: Topic similarity does not prove direct adjacency.
common_mistakes.correction: Prefer a precise grammatical or logical link such as noun-pronoun, claim-example, cause-result, or event-consequence.

common_mistakes.mistake: Starting with a sentence beginning 'however', 'therefore', or 'for example'.
common_mistakes.why_it_fails: These markers normally depend on an earlier idea.
common_mistakes.correction: Identify the statement being contrasted, the cause producing the result, or the generalization being illustrated.

common_mistakes.mistake: Trying to solve the entire order in one mental step.
common_mistakes.why_it_fails: Several sentences may fit the general topic, creating unnecessary uncertainty.
common_mistakes.correction: Form strong adjacent pairs first and then connect those pairs.

common_mistakes.mistake: Using only grammar and ignoring meaning.
common_mistakes.why_it_fails: Two sentences may be grammatically compatible but logically unrelated.
common_mistakes.correction: Require both grammatical cohesion and sensible development of ideas.

common_mistakes.mistake: Using only meaning and ignoring reference words.
common_mistakes.why_it_fails: A broadly logical sequence can still contain an unresolved pronoun or definite noun phrase.
common_mistakes.correction: Perform a final reference audit for every pronoun, demonstrative, and definite noun phrase.

common_mistakes.mistake: Placing a conclusion before the evidence.
common_mistakes.why_it_fails: Expressions such as 'overall', 'therefore', and 'these findings suggest' normally summarize earlier material.
common_mistakes.correction: Identify what evidence or discussion the conclusion depends on.

common_mistakes.why_it_fails: The resulting order may reverse a historical event or scientific process.
common_mistakes.correction: Create a simple timeline and check words such as 'initially', 'later', 'after', and 'eventually'.

common_mistakes.why_it_fails: Late changes based on intuition can destroy strong links and waste shared Reading time.
common_mistakes.correction: Stop once the opening, each adjacent pair, and the global flow all have clear evidence.

practice_plan.name: Concept and clue review
activities: Review the difference between a topic sentence and a supporting sentence.
Classify sample sentences as introduction, explanation, example, result, contrast, or conclusion.
Underline all articles, pronouns, demonstratives, and discourse markers.
Explain whether each marked word points backward, forward, or simply adds information.
practice_plan.success_target: Correctly identify the role and dependency of at least 8 out of 10 sample sentences.

practice_plan.name: Article and referent drills
activities: Match sentences containing 'a' or a proper name with later sentences containing 'the'.
Match pronouns with singular or plural antecedents.
Match demonstrative phrases such as 'this result' and 'these findings' with the ideas they summarize.
Reject pairs containing an unresolved or illogical reference.
practice_plan.success_target: Form at least 8 correct sentence pairs and explain the reference in each pair.

practice_plan.name: Discourse-marker drills
activities: Sort linkers by addition, contrast, example, result, sequence, and conclusion.
Write the type of sentence that must normally precede each linker.
Reconstruct four mini-paragraphs containing one strong discourse marker.
Replace each marker with another expression serving the same function.
practice_plan.success_target: Recognize the function of at least 90 percent of the target linkers.

practice_plan.name: Guided paragraph reconstruction
activities: Complete three untimed Re-order paragraphs.
Label the opening candidate and every dependent sentence.
Record the strongest adjacent pairs before writing the final order.
Compare the final order with the answer and identify the clue missed in any incorrect link.
practice_plan.success_target: Produce a fully justified sequence for at least two of the three items.

practice_plan.name: Timed practice set
activities: Complete four Re-order paragraph items under self-imposed time limits.
Use the OPEN-PAIR-CHAIN-CHECK method without skipping the final audit.
Record time spent and confidence level for each item.
Avoid spending excessive time on one uncertain connection.
practice_plan.success_target: Maintain accuracy while completing each item in approximately two to three minutes during practice.

practice_plan.name: Error analysis and repair
activities: Compare each response with the correct sequence.
Classify every mistake as opening, article, referent, discourse, chronology, lexical chain, or global logic.
Rewrite the explanation for the correct adjacent pair.
Create one personal rule for the most frequent error category.
practice_plan.success_target: Explain the exact reason for every incorrect placement rather than recording only the correct answer.

practice_plan.name: Mixed review
activities: Complete one final item without notes.
State the opening clue, strongest pair, and final transition.
Read the completed paragraph aloud to test natural flow.
Update the mastery checklist.
practice_plan.success_target: Complete the final item with a coherent order and at least three explicit supporting clues.

mastery_checklist: I can identify a sentence that introduces the topic without relying on earlier information.
I can distinguish a topic sentence from examples, evidence, explanations, and conclusions.
I can use 'a' or 'an' as a possible first-mention clue and 'the' as a possible later-reference clue.
I do not rely on articles alone when the meaning suggests a different order.
I can match singular and plural pronouns with compatible antecedents.
I can explain what phrases such as 'this result', 'that approach', and 'these findings' refer to.
I can recognize addition, contrast, example, cause-effect, sequence, and conclusion markers.
I can identify chronological and procedural order from tense and time expressions.
I can recognize lexical chains formed by repetition, synonymy, and general-specific relationships.
I can form strong adjacent pairs before deciding the full sequence.
I can reject an order containing an unexplained pronoun or definite noun phrase.
I can reject an order that places an example before its general claim.
I can reject an order that places a result before its cause.
I can read the completed paragraph and confirm that the argument develops smoothly.
I can explain why my chosen order is correct using specific textual clues.
I can complete the task efficiently without allowing one item to consume too much Reading-section time.

strategy_notes.title: Use evidence strength
strategy_notes.note: Rank clues by reliability. Exact reference links and explicit sequence markers are usually stronger than broad topic similarity or what merely sounds natural.

strategy_notes.title: Distinguish local and global cohesion
strategy_notes.note: A pair may connect grammatically but still sit in the wrong part of the paragraph. After forming pairs, confirm that the whole text develops logically.

strategy_notes.title: Search for mandatory predecessors
strategy_notes.note: Sentences beginning with 'this', 'these', 'the', 'however', 'therefore', or 'for example' often reveal what kind of sentence must come before them.

strategy_notes.title: Do not overvalue the first sentence
strategy_notes.note: Finding the opening is important, but the rest of the order still depends on sentence-to-sentence cohesion. A correct first box does not guarantee a correct chain.

strategy_notes.title: Use paragraph architecture
strategy_notes.note: Common structures include general-to-specific, claim-evidence-interpretation, problem-solution-evaluation, cause-effect, comparison-contrast, and chronological sequence.

strategy_notes.title: Treat definitions carefully
strategy_notes.note: A definition normally follows the first appearance of a technical term, while a later example or application follows the definition.

strategy_notes.title: Check renamed information
strategy_notes.note: A noun may be repeated through a broader label: 'the Burj Dubai' can become 'the building', and 'a hotel' can become 'that accommodation'.

strategy_notes.title: Use punctuation as supporting evidence
strategy_notes.note: Punctuation can reveal sentence function, but it should support rather than replace grammatical and logical analysis.

strategy_notes.title: Protect shared Reading time
strategy_notes.note: Re-order paragraphs are not individually timed, so use a personal time limit and move on when the sequence has strong evidence.

strategy_notes.title: Review adjacent links
strategy_notes.note: Before submitting, justify every boundary: why does sentence 2 follow sentence 1, why does sentence 3 follow sentence 2, and so on?

strategy_notes.title: Learn from partial structures
strategy_notes.note: Even when the whole order is uncertain, identifying strong adjacent pairs improves the quality of the attempt and builds the core skill tested by the task.

strategy_notes.title: Keep a clue-error log
strategy_notes.note: After practice, record whether errors came from articles, pronouns, discourse markers, chronology, paragraph role, or overreliance on intuition.

key_terms.definition: A reading item type in which jumbled text boxes must be arranged into the single coherent order intended by the writer.
A sentence that introduces the paragraph's central topic or controlling idea.
A sentence that develops the main idea through explanation, evidence, examples, comparison, or consequences.
A word or phrase that signals a relationship such as addition, contrast, result, example, sequence, or conclusion.
A word or phrase, such as a pronoun or demonstrative expression, that points to information mentioned elsewhere in the text.
The earlier noun, phrase, or idea to which a pronoun or other reference expression refers.
The grammatical and lexical connections that link sentences into a unified text.
The overall logical and meaningful development of ideas in a text.

source_scope.items_from_source: Two to three Re-order paragraphs items
source_scope.timing_note: Reading items are completed within a shared section time rather than being timed individually.
